prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology and active form of glucagon-like peptide-1 that made incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for B016 to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The discovery chain is original and mechanistically clear (proglucagon processing, the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, insulinotropic action in humans). It has been independently confirmed for decades and now underpins drugs with large effects on glycaemia, weight and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. The chair asked whether a prize for discovery should separate the active peptide from long-acting analogues. I think it should, because the prize rewards the step that defined the biological target and its physiology. Analogue engineering, however skilful, worked on an already defined target. The citation therefore stops at the physiology and active form and names the therapies as their consequence. I also considered a second part and rejected it. Every candidate for a second part (B010, B044, B003, B023) brings its own attribution problem or a less mature link to medicine, while B016 is mature and well delimited. Adding a part would not strengthen the scientific case and would add credit risk.
statement.case_against: Attribution is still the weak point, and the round-1 exchange has not removed it. Knudsen's acylated analogue is what turned the biology into a usable medicine, so the trio can be read as passing over the person without whom patients would not benefit. The priority record for the active peptide, including Habener's contribution, is outside the credit list and cannot be verified from the files I may use. I am working from recollection there and cannot treat it as evidence. The citation wording and the choice of Mojsov over Knudsen carry real judgement, and I accept that a reasonable member could draw the line differently. Long-term safety of chronic incretin therapy is still accumulating, as the chair notes, although I do not think it bears on the discovery.

responses.point: Sandberg now prefers Holst, Drucker and Knudsen, with a citation that includes development of long-acting therapies, while still regarding the unfolded protein response as the scientifically cleanest discovery on the list.
responses.response: I take your argument seriously that the prize should recognise how the biology became a durable drug. But I still disagree on the third name. A citation that covers development puts the committee in the position of judging an industrial programme. It also leaves the identification of the active peptide without a laureate, even though every later step depends on it. I would rather keep the citation on physiology and the active form and let the therapies stand as the consequence. On the UPR, I agree it is the cleanest two-person credit, and it stays on my alternatives. I do not rank it above GLP-1, because GLP-1 already shows its impact in patients and its attribution, though imperfect, is better delimited than most of the list.

responses.point: Linnarsson's round-1 file names Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, although several openings described him as preferring Knudsen, and he treats the UPR as the cleaner credit story if GLP-1 allocation stalls.
responses.response: Your configuration now matches mine, which helps with the chair's counting question, and I read it as a considered move to Mojsov and not as consensus by default. I agree with your reservation that the clinical story can overshadow the physiological discovery the citation should honour. That is a further reason to word the citation around physiology and the active peptide. On the fallback, I would use UPR only if the GLP-1 allocation truly cannot be settled. Our disagreement over Mojsov versus Knudsen is a matter of judgement and not a gap in evidence, so I do not think it is a reason to abandon a mature discovery.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius asks that the scientific case for GLP-1 be tested and not assumed, and she has moved from Knudsen to Mojsov because the prize is for discovery.
responses.response: I accept the challenge and have tested the case on originality, independent confirmation and lasting impact. On those terms it holds without relying on the opening ranking. The physiology was worked out step by step and replicated by many groups, and the therapeutic effects are shown in randomised trials. I share your concern that the clinical product owes a great deal to industrial development. The answer in my view is to be explicit that the prize is for the physiology and the active peptide, not to enlarge the trio. I would not describe the choice as free of cost, and the omission of Knudsen should be acknowledged in the committee's reasoning.

responses.point: The chair asks whether a second prize part (UPR, optogenetics, TOR or CAR-T) should be added, and notes that long-term safety and durability of incretin therapy are still accumulating.
responses.response: I would keep GLP-1 as a single part. A two-part prize would only be justified if the second part were as mature and as cleanly credited as GLP-1, and I do not think any is. Optogenetics is the case closest to my own field. I do not let that familiarity count in its favour, and I still see no three-name allocation that excludes Boyden, Bamberg and Miesenböck defensibly. UPR is the strongest second part scientifically, but I do not see a benefit that outweighs the added debate. On safety, I agree it is still accumulating, but it concerns the drugs and not the physiology we would be crediting. Pending data should not delay the recognition of the discovery.

uncertainties: Whether Habener's contribution to the priority record of the active GLP-1 peptide should change the three-name configuration. I cannot verify it from the files I may use.
Whether the majority will accept Mojsov over Knudsen as the third name, given the objection that the prize then bypasses the person who made the medicine practical.
Whether the committee will want a second part. If it does, I think B010 is the more defensible choice, with Walter and Mori.
Whether the optogenetics attribution problem (six credited names) has any defensible three-person solution.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my round-1 disclosure. I co-authored a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann, a fellow committee member, on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons, which does not touch any shortlisted ballot, and I request no recusal. I work in neuroscience, a field near optogenetics (B044), but I have no documented involvement with its credited individuals, and I will disclose any link that emerges.
